verify_note: Criteria transcribed for coaching use. Verify wording and marks against the current IB Economics Guide before high-stakes use.

requirements: Each commentary uses a different key concept as a lens
Each commentary is based on a different unit of the syllabus
Articles come from three different sources
Each article was published no earlier than one year before the commentary was written
Each commentary is no more than 800 words

criteria.name: Diagrams
criteria.asks: Are relevant, accurate, correctly labelled diagrams included and fully explained?
coach_checklist: Diagram is relevant to the article's central economic issue
Axes, curves and equilibria are fully and correctly labelled
The text explains the diagram: what shifts, why, and what the new outcome is
The diagram uses the article's specifics (real prices, goods, actors) not generic P/Q

criteria.name: Terminology
criteria.asks: Is relevant economic terminology used appropriately throughout?
coach_checklist: Terms are defined the first time they carry analytical weight
Terms are used precisely (e.g. demand vs quantity demanded)
Terminology appears throughout, not clustered in one definitions paragraph

criteria.name: Application and key concept
criteria.asks: Is relevant economic theory, and the chosen key concept, applied to the article throughout?
coach_checklist: Theory is tied to named actors, numbers and events from the article
One key concept is explicitly chosen and used as a lens, not name-dropped
No paragraph is pure textbook theory with no article link

criteria.name: Analysis
criteria.asks: Is relevant economic theory explained with effective, developed chains of reasoning linked to the article?
coach_checklist: Cause-and-effect chains are complete (A → B → C, no jumps)
The 'why' behind each shift or outcome is explained, not asserted
Analysis follows from the diagram rather than running parallel to it

criteria.name: Evaluation
criteria.asks: Are judgments made and supported by reasoned arguments (synthesis of the analysis)?
coach_checklist: Considers at least two of: stakeholders, short run vs long run, magnitude/significance, assumptions and their limits, counterarguments
Judgments are argued from the analysis, not bolted on in the last paragraph
Reaches a supported conclusion rather than 'it depends' with no direction
